text:
Need
R function or example




Mean, sample standard deviation, sample variance
mean(x), sd(x), var(x)


Sample size and square root
length(x), sqrt(x)


Normal critical value
qnorm(0.975)


Tukey studentized-range critical value
qtukey(0.95, nmeans=4, df=20)


Fisher LSD from raw data and a fitted ANOVA
agricolae::LSD.test() (requires the agricolae package)






The statistical procedure determines which distribution to use. Use the same distribution and degrees of freedom when finding a critical value or a p-value for that test.









Statistical procedure
Distribution
Critical value function
P-value function




Two-proportion test; two independent means with known population standard deviations
Standard normal (\(z\))
qnorm()
pnorm()


Paired differences; two independent means with unknown population standard deviations; Fisher’s LSD
\(t\)
qt()
pt()


Comparing two population variances; one-way or two-way ANOVA
\(F\)
qf()
pf()


Tukey multiple comparisons
Studentized range
qtukey()
ptukey()



How to read the function names: Functions beginning with q return a critical value (a cutoff on the horizontal axis) when you provide a probability. Functions beginning with p return a probability (area under the curve) when you provide a calculated test statistic. By default, R uses the area to the left of the input. lower.tail=FALSE requests the area to the right.



The alternative hypothesis determines the tail. Interpret the sign relative to how you defined Population 1, Population 2, or the paired difference.









Wording of the alternative hypothesis
Test direction
Area for a p-value
Rejection region




Less than (\(<\))
Left-tailed
Left of the observed statistic
Statistic below the lower critical value


Greater than (\(>\))
Right-tailed
Right of the observed statistic
Statistic above the upper critical value


Different (\(\ne\))
Two-tailed
Both tails
Statistic beyond either critical value



Exception to remember: ANOVA \(F\) tests are always right-tailed, even though the alternative states that means differ. For an \(F\) test comparing two population variances, the alternative can be left-, right-, or two-tailed.



Use the significance level alpha and the relevant degrees of freedom. For a two-tailed \(z\) or \(t\) test, split alpha equally between the two tails.








Test direction
Standard normal (\(z\))
\(t\) distribution




Left-tailed
qnorm(alpha)
qt(alpha, df)


Right-tailed
qnorm(1-alpha)
qt(1-alpha, df)


Two-tailed: lower cutoff
qnorm(alpha/2)
qt(alpha/2, df)


Two-tailed: upper cutoff
qnorm(1-alpha/2)
qt(1-alpha/2, df)



For \(F\) procedures, use the numerator and denominator degrees of freedom in the same order as the F statistic:







\(F\) procedure
Critical value calculation




Compare variances: left-tailed
qf(alpha, df1, df2)


Compare variances: right-tailed
qf(1-alpha, df1, df2)


Compare variances: two-tailed lower cutoff
qf(alpha/2, df1, df2)


Compare variances: two-tailed upper cutoff
qf(1-alpha/2, df1, df2)


ANOVA: right-tailed
qf(1-alpha, df_effect, df_error)



For Tukey HSD, use qtukey(1-alpha, nmeans=k, df=df_error) to find the studentized-range critical value for the set of group comparisons. Fisher’s LSD uses a two-tailed \(t\) cutoff: qt(1-alpha/2, df_error).
Example of interpreting alpha: At alpha <- 0.05, a right-tailed test puts 0.05 in the right tail (1-alpha = 0.95 is to the left). A two-tailed test puts 0.025 in each tail (alpha/2 = 0.025).



After calculating your test statistic, choose the same distribution and tail as the hypothesis test.








Test direction
Normal (\(z\))
\(t\)




Left-tailed
pnorm(z_stat)
pt(t_stat, df)


Right-tailed
pnorm(z_stat, lower.tail=FALSE)
pt(t_stat, df, lower.tail=FALSE)


Two-tailed
2*pnorm(-abs(z_stat))
2*pt(-abs(t_stat), df)










\(F\) procedure and direction
P-value calculation




Compare variances: left-tailed
pf(F_stat, df1, df2)


Compare variances: right-tailed
pf(F_stat, df1, df2, lower.tail=FALSE)


Compare variances: two-tailed
min(1, 2*min(pf(F_stat,df1,df2), pf(F_stat,df1,df2,lower.tail=FALSE)))


ANOVA: right-tailed
pf(F_stat, df_effect, df_error, lower.tail=FALSE)



The two-tailed variance-test calculation doubles the smaller tail probability. The \(F\) distribution is asymmetric, so do not use the normal or \(t\) two-tailed shortcut with an \(F\) statistic. In a Tukey analysis, TukeyHSD(fitted_model) reports adjusted pairwise p-values when a suitable raw-data model is available.










Comparison
Decision




p_value <= alpha
Reject \(H_0\); sufficient evidence for the alternative hypothesis


p_value > alpha
Fail to reject \(H_0\); insufficient evidence for the alternative hypothesis



A corresponding two-sided confidence interval excludes the null value when the test rejects at the matching significance level. The null value is 0 for a mean or proportion difference and 1 for a population variance ratio.
Quick check: For an \(F\) test comparing variances, \(F=s_1^2/s_2^2\). For an ANOVA \(F\) test, \(F=MS_{\text{effect}}/MSE\). Keep full precision until the final answer unless the problem explicitly requires using a rounded intermediate result.

title: Exam 2 Study Guide
text:
1. Paired Difference Test
Use when observations belong together, such as before/after values on the same people. Define the difference in the order requested. After that, work with one sample of differences.

Formulas
Where \(n\) is the number of pairs:
\[d_i=x_{1i}-x_{2i},\qquad \bar d=\frac{\sum d_i}{n},\qquad s_d=\sqrt{\frac{\sum(d_i-\bar d)^2}{n-1}}\]
\[SE=\frac{s_d}{\sqrt n},\qquad t=\frac{\bar d-\mu_{d,0}}{SE},\qquad df=n-1\]
\[\text{Confidence interval: }\bar d\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\,SE\]


Common Questions and How to Approach Them








If the problem asks…
What to do
R code




Is this a paired difference design?
Determine whether each observation has a corresponding observation in the other condition.
No calculation needed


What are the paired differences?
Subtract the two measurements within each pair, keeping the order consistent.
d <- x1 - x2


What is the mean difference?
Find the average of the differences.
mean(d)


What is the standard deviation of the differences?
Calculate the sample standard deviation of the differences.
sd(d)


What are the degrees of freedom?
Subtract 1 from the number of pairs.
length(d) - 1


What is the critical t value?
Use the confidence level or significance level and the degrees of freedom.
qt(1 - alpha/2, df)


What is the confidence interval?
Calculate the mean difference plus or minus the margin of error.
mean(d) + c(-1, 1) * qt(1-alpha/2, df) * sd(d)/sqrt(length(d))


What is the test statistic?
Divide the difference between the observed and hypothesized mean difference by the standard error.
(mean(d) - 0) / (sd(d)/sqrt(length(d)))


What is the p-value?
Use pt() with the correct tail.
pt(t_stat, df) for a left-tailed test


What is the conclusion?
Compare the p-value with the significance level.
Reject H0 if p_value <= alpha



Remember: The order of subtraction determines the meaning of a positive or negative difference. For a paired test, the standard deviation is calculated from the differences.


Choosing the Correct Hypothesis








Wording of the question
Alternative hypothesis
Test direction




Has increased
\(H_a:\mu_d>0\)
Right-tailed


Has decreased
\(H_a:\mu_d<0\)
Left-tailed


Has changed or is different
\(H_a:\mu_d\ne0\)
Two-tailed



These directions assume that the paired differences are defined as the measurement of interest minus its comparison measurement.


Example: Paired Before-and-After Measurements

before/after scores. Suppose d = after - before. A positive mean difference represents an increase. The same setup supports questions asking for the differences, their SD, a confidence interval, or a hypothesis-test decision.


before <- c(65, 70, 68, 74, 73)
after  <- c(69, 74, 69, 80, 78)
d <- after - before
mean(d)                      # Mean difference

[1] 4

sd(d)                        # SD of differences

[1] 1.870829

n <- length(d)
se <- sd(d)/sqrt(n)

# Two-sided 95% confidence interval
alpha <- 0.05
t_star <- qt(1-alpha/2, df=n-1)
mean(d) + c(-1, 1)*t_star*se

[1] 1.677059 6.322941

# Example hypothesis: mean difference > 0 (an increase)
t_stat <- mean(d)/se
t_stat

[1] 4.780914

pt(t_stat, df=n-1, lower.tail=FALSE)

[1] 0.00438483

# With paired raw data, R can also calculate the test directly:
t.test(after, before, paired=TRUE, alternative="greater")


    Paired t-test

data:  after and before
t = 4.7809, df = 4, p-value = 0.004385
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is greater than 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.216369      Inf
sample estimates:
mean difference 
              4 


Remember: The normality assumption concerns the paired differences. For a change in either direction, use a two-tailed test; for a specified increase/decrease, select the tail using the sign of the defined difference.

title: Exam 2 Study Guide
text:
2. Two Independent Population Means
When comparing the means of two separate groups, check whether the population standard deviations are known and whether equal variances are assumed. When the population variances are unknown but assumed equal, use a pooled two-sample t test. Keep the subtraction as Population 1 minus Population 2.

Formulas
\[s_p^2=\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2},\qquad SE=s_p\sqrt{\frac1{n_1}+\frac1{n_2}}\]
\[t=\frac{(\bar x_1-\bar x_2)-\Delta_0}{SE},\qquad df=n_1+n_2-2\]
When population standard deviations are known, use a two-sample \(z\) procedure with \(SE=\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1+\sigma_2^2/n_2}\) and pnorm(). When equal variances are not assumed, use Welch’s \(t\) procedure with \(SE=\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}\); with raw observations, t.test(group1, group2, var.equal=FALSE) computes the Welch test. The example here illustrates the pooled procedure.


Common Questions and How to Approach Them








If the problem asks…
What to do
R code




Are the samples independent?
Determine whether the observations come from two separate, unrelated groups.
No calculation needed


What is the difference between sample means?
Subtract Population 2’s mean from Population 1’s mean.
xbar1 - xbar2


Which procedure should be used?
Check whether population standard deviations are known and whether equal variances are assumed.
See lecture formulas


What is the pooled variance?
Combine the sample variances using their degrees of freedom when equal variances are assumed.
((n1-1)*s1^2+(n2-1)*s2^2)/(n1+n2-2)


What is the standard error?
Use the formula for the appropriate z or t procedure.
See lecture formulas


What are the pooled degrees of freedom?
Add the sample sizes and subtract 2.
n1+n2-2


What is the test statistic?
Subtract the hypothesized difference from the observed difference, then divide by the standard error.
(xbar1-xbar2-D0)/SE


What is the critical value?
Use qnorm() for z or qt() for t.
qt(1-alpha/2, df) for a two-tailed t test


What is the p-value?
Use pnorm() or pt() with the appropriate tail.
2*pt(-abs(t_stat), df) for a two-tailed t test


What is the confidence interval?
Calculate the difference in means plus or minus the margin of error.
(xbar1-xbar2)+c(-1,1)*qt(1-alpha/2,df)*SE


What is the conclusion?
Compare the p-value with alpha.
Reject H0 if p_value <= alpha





Choosing the Correct Hypothesis








Wording of the question
Alternative hypothesis
Test direction




Population 1 has a higher mean
\(H_a:\mu_1>\mu_2\)
Right-tailed


Population 1 has a lower mean
\(H_a:\mu_1<\mu_2\)
Left-tailed


The population means differ
\(H_a:\mu_1\ne\mu_2\)
Two-tailed



Remember: The order of subtraction matters. Keep Population 1 minus Population 2 consistent throughout the calculations. When equal population variances are assumed, use the pooled two-sample t procedure.


Example: Pooled Two-Sample t Test

Two independent delivery teams. Team A has \(n_1=18\), mean 42.5 minutes, SD 5.1; Team B has \(n_2=15\), mean 45.0 minutes, SD 6.3. Assume equal population variances and test whether the means differ.


n1 <- 18; xbar1 <- 42.5; s1 <- 5.1
n2 <- 15; xbar2 <- 45.0; s2 <- 6.3
sp2 <- ((n1-1)*s1^2 + (n2-1)*s2^2)/(n1+n2-2)
se <- sqrt(sp2*(1/n1+1/n2))
t_stat <- (xbar1-xbar2)/se
t_stat

[1] -1.260426

2*pt(-abs(t_stat), df=n1+n2-2)  # Two-sided p-value

[1] 0.2169208


If raw observations are provided, t.test(group1, group2, var.equal=TRUE) implements the pooled t procedure. If the problem states unequal variances, use the Welch procedure from the lecture instead.

title: Exam 2 Study Guide
text:
3. Comparing Two Population Proportions
Use for two independent groups when the outcome is a count or percentage (e.g., defective versus not defective). Set Population 1 and Population 2 in the order stated. A difference of 0.03 is 3 percentage points.

Formulas
\[\hat p_1=\frac{x_1}{n_1},\qquad\hat p_2=\frac{x_2}{n_2},\qquad\hat p=\frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2}\]
For a test of \(H_0:p_1=p_2\), pool the proportions:
\[z=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}\]
For a confidence interval, do not pool:
\[ (\hat p_1-\hat p_2)\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_1(1-\hat p_1)}{n_1}+\frac{\hat p_2(1-\hat p_2)}{n_2}}\]


Common Questions and How to Approach Them








If the problem asks…
What to do
R code




What are the sample proportions?
Divide the number of successes by the sample size for each group.
p1 <- x1/n1 and p2 <- x2/n2


What is the difference between proportions?
Subtract Population 2 from Population 1.
p1 - p2


What is the pooled proportion?
Combine the successes and sample sizes from both groups.
(x1 + x2)/(n1 + n2)


What is the standard error for a hypothesis test?
Use the pooled proportion when testing equality.
sqrt(p_pool*(1-p_pool)*(1/n1+1/n2))


What is the z test statistic?
Divide the observed difference by the pooled standard error.
(p1-p2)/SE


What is the p-value?
Use pnorm() with the appropriate tail.
pnorm(z_stat) for a left-tailed test


What is the confidence interval?
Use the separate, unpooled sample proportions to calculate the standard error.
See formula above


What does the confidence interval indicate?
Determine whether zero is included in the interval.
No additional calculation needed



The unpooled confidence-interval formula is given above. In the example below, the same inputs can be used to calculate the pooled test statistic or the unpooled confidence interval.


Choosing the Alternative Hypothesis








Wording
Alternative hypothesis
Tail




Population 1 has a larger proportion
\(H_a:p_1>p_2\)
Right


Population 1 has a smaller proportion
\(H_a:p_1<p_2\)
Left


The proportions differ
\(H_a:p_1\ne p_2\)
Two





Example: Proportion Test and Confidence Interval

Defective phones. Plant A has 8 defective phones in 200; Plant B has 10 in 200. This template answers requests for sample proportions, pooled estimate, \(z\), p-value, or a confidence interval.


x1 <- 8; n1 <- 200
x2 <- 10; n2 <- 200
alpha <- 0.05
p1 <- x1/n1; p2 <- x2/n2
p1; p2

[1] 0.04


[1] 0.05

# Hypothesis test: H_a: p1 < p2
pooled <- (x1+x2)/(n1+n2)
se_test <- sqrt(pooled*(1-pooled)*(1/n1+1/n2))
z_stat <- (p1-p2)/se_test
z_stat

[1] -0.4823831

pnorm(z_stat)                   # Left-tailed p-value

[1] 0.3147669

# Confidence interval: p1 - p2 (unpooled)
se_ci <- sqrt(p1*(1-p1)/n1 + p2*(1-p2)/n2)
(p1-p2) + c(-1,1)*qnorm(1-alpha/2)*se_ci

[1] -0.05061904  0.03061904


Check counts of successes and failures for both groups. The lecture’s normal-approximation guideline is at least 5 of each in each group. A confidence interval that contains 0 is compatible with equal proportions at the corresponding two-sided significance level.

title: Exam 2 Study Guide
text:
4. Comparing Two Population Variances
Use when comparing variation, spread, or variances, with independent samples from approximately normal populations. The numerator must correspond to Population 1.

Formulas
\[F=\frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2},\qquad df_1=n_1-1,\quad df_2=n_2-1\]
If the problem provides standard deviations, square them to obtain variances. For a confidence interval estimating \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\), define \(R=s_1^2/s_2^2\):
\[\left(\frac{R}{F_{1-\alpha/2;df_1,df_2}},\;\frac{R}{F_{\alpha/2;df_1,df_2}}\right)\]


Common Questions and How to Approach Them








If the problem asks…
What to do
R code




What is the variance ratio?
Divide the variance of Population 1 by the variance of Population 2.

6. Multiple Comparison Procedures
After a significant overall ANOVA, pairwise comparisons can help identify which means differ. Pay attention to whether the question specifies Fisher’s LSD or Tukey’s HSD, as their thresholds differ.

Fisher’s LSD
Fisher’s LSD for means \(i\) and \(j\):
\[LSD=t_{1-\alpha/2,\,df_E}\sqrt{MSE\left(\frac1{n_i}+\frac1{n_j}\right)}\]
A pair is significantly different when \(|\bar x_i-\bar x_j|>LSD\). The corresponding pairwise confidence interval is \((\bar x_i-\bar x_j)\pm LSD\).


Tukey’s HSD
Tukey’s HSD for equal group sizes \(n\):
\[HSD=q_{1-\alpha;k,df_E}\sqrt{\frac{MSE}{n}}\]
For unequal group sizes, the Tukey-Kramer pairwise margin is \(q_{1-\alpha;k,df_E}\sqrt{MSE(1/n_i+1/n_j)/2}\). The Tukey confidence interval is the observed pairwise difference \(\pm\) this margin.


Common Questions and How to Approach Them








If the problem asks…
What to do
R code

Which treatment pairs differ?

What is the Tukey studentized-range critical value?
Use the number of groups and error degrees of freedom.
qtukey(1-alpha, k, df_error)


What is a Tukey confidence interval?
Calculate the mean difference plus or minus Tukey’s margin.
See formula above


Does the Tukey interval show a significant difference?
Determine whether the interval includes zero.
Compare interval endpoints with zero

Decision: For a pairwise confidence interval, if 0 is outside the interval, that pair differs significantly at the specified level. When raw observations are available, fit aov() and use TukeyHSD(model) for Tukey comparisons.

8. Two-Way ANOVA: Factorial Design
Use when the study considers two factors of interest, such as teaching method and study schedule, with repeated observations in their combinations. A factorial ANOVA tests Factor A, Factor B, and their interaction.

where \(x_i\) is each observation and \(w_i\) is its corresponding weight.

title: Exam 1 Formula Guide
text:
Two Variables

Covariance
The sample covariance is:
\[
s_{xy}
=
\frac{\sum (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{n-1}
\]
A positive covariance indicates that the variables tend to move in the same direction, while a negative covariance indicates that they tend to move in opposite directions.

x <- c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5.5, 6)
y <- c(63,  66, 69, 72, 78, 81, 84, 87, 90, 96)

# x
xbar <- mean(x)
xn   <- length(x)
xSD  <- sqrt( (sum((x - xbar)^2)) / (length(x)-1) ) # sample is n - 1

# y
ybar <- mean(y)
ySD  <- sqrt( (sum((y - ybar)^2)) / (length(y)-1) ) # sample is n - 1
yn   <- length(y)

# covariance
covariance <- (sum((x - xbar)*(y - ybar)) / (length(x)-1) )

covariance


# using data
cov(x = data$x, y = data$y)

# using vectors
cov(x, y)



Correlation Coefficient
The correlation coefficient can be calculated from the covariance and standard deviations:
\[
r = \frac{s_{xy}}{s_xs_y}
\]
where \(s_{xy}\) is the sample covariance and \(s_x\) and \(s_y\) are the sample standard deviations.

# REQUIRED: Use the covariance section above AND run it !
# Then, calculate r
r <- covariance / (xSD * ySD)
r


# using data
cor(x = data$x, y = data$y)

# using vectors
cor(x, y)

text:
Uniform Distribution

Identification
Problem gives:

the variable is uniformly distributed
values lie between \(a\) and \(b\)
every value in the interval is equally likely



Key formulas
Mean:
\[
\mu = \frac{a+b}{2}
\]
Standard deviation
\[
\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}}
\]
Probability to the right of a cutoff:
\[
P(X > x) = \frac{b-x}{b-a}
\]
Probability to the left of a cutoff:
\[
P(X < x) = \frac{x-a}{b-a}
\]


Example script

# mean and standard deviation
mu <- (a + b) / 2
sigma <- sqrt((b - a)^2 / 12)

# probability greater than x
(b - x) / (b - a)

# probability less than x
(x - a) / (b - a)

section: Normal distribution with a single raw score
text:
Normal distribution with a single raw score

Identification
Problem gives:

a mean and standard deviation
says that the variable is normally distributed
asks about a randomly selected observation
uses \(X\) rather than \(\bar{x}\)



Key formulas
For a value between two numbers:
\[
P(a < X < b)
\]
Standardizing:
\[
P(a < X < b)
\]
For a value above a cutoff:
\[
P(X > x)
\]
For a value below a cutoff:
\[
P(X < x)
\]
For finding a cutoff from a percentile:
\[
P(X \le x) = p
\]
For solving for standard deviation:
\[
z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\qquad \Rightarrow \qquad\sigma = \frac{x - \mu}{z}
\]


Example script 

# between two values
pnorm(upper, mean = mu, sd = sigma) - 
  pnorm(lower, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# greater than
1 - pnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# less than
pnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# cutoff from a percentile
qnorm(p, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# solve for sigma
z <- qnorm(p_left)
sigma <- (x - mu) / z

title: exam3
text:
Sampling distribution of the mean \(\bar{X}\)

Identification
Problem gives:

“sample mean”
“a random sample of \(n\)”
“what is the probability that the sample mean…”
“sampling distribution”



Key formulas
Mean of the sampling distribution:
\[
\mu_{\bar{X}} = \mu
\]
Standard deviation of the sampling distribution, also called the standard error:
\[
\sigma_{\bar{X}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
If variance is given first:
\[
\sigma = \sqrt{\text{variance}}\\
\sigma_{\bar{X}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
Probability forms:
\[
P(\bar{X} < x)\\
P(\bar{X} > x)\\
P\bigl(|\bar{X} - \mu| < a\bigr)\\
P\bigl(|\bar{X} - \mu| > a\bigr)
\]
Expanded interval forms:
\[
P(\mu - a < \bar{X} < \mu + a)\\
P(\bar{X} < \mu - a) + P(\bar{X} > \mu + a)
\]


Example script

# if variance is given
sigma <- sqrt(variance)

# standard error
se <- sigma / sqrt(n)

# less than
pnorm(xbar, mean = mu, sd = se)

# greater than
1 - pnorm(xbar, mean = mu, sd = se)

# within a distance of mu
pnorm(mu + amount, mean = mu, sd = se) -
  pnorm(mu - amount, mean = mu, sd = se)

# greater than a distance from mu
1 - (pnorm(mu + amount, mean = mu, sd = se) -
       pnorm(mu - amount, mean = mu, sd = se))

text:
4. Confidence Interval for a Population Mean

When \(\sigma\) Is Known
\[
\bar{x}\pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
z_critical <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2)

margin_error <- z_critical * sigma / sqrt(n)

lower <- xbar - margin_error
upper <- xbar + margin_error


When \(\sigma\) Is Unknown
\[
\bar{x}\pm t_{\alpha/2,df}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
with:
\[
df=n-1
\]
df <- n - 1

t_critical <- qt(1 - alpha / 2, df)

margin_error <- t_critical * s / sqrt(n)

lower <- xbar - margin_error
upper <- xbar + margin_error

c(lower = lower, upper = upper)


CI for a Two-Tailed Test
For:
\[
H_0:\mu=\mu_0
\]

If \(\mu_0\) is inside the confidence interval, fail to reject \(H_0\).
If \(\mu_0\) is outside the confidence interval, reject \(H_0\).

5. One-Proportion \(z\) Test
Use when testing a population proportion.

Sample Proportion
\[
\hat{p}=\frac{x}{n}
\]
p_hat <- x / n
where \(x\) is the number with the characteristic of interest.


Check the Conditions
Both should be at least 5:
\[
np_0\ge5
\]
\[
n(1-p_0)\ge5
\]
n * p0
n * (1 - p0)


Test Statistic
\[
z=
\frac{\hat{p}-p_0}
{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}}
\]
z <- (p_hat - p0) /
     sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n)
Then use the same pnorm() commands as any other \(z\) test:
# Left-tailed
pnorm(z)

# Right-tailed
1 - pnorm(z)
pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Two-tailed
2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z)))
